formulas.name: SUVAT: velocity after time t

variables.name: acceleration
variables.description: Constant acceleration (negative if slowing down in the positive direction).

formulas.explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. If it is constant, the velocity changes by a every second, so after t seconds it has changed by a t. This is the definition of acceleration rearranged.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for constant acceleration problems that do not involve the displacement s.

example.story: A car speeds up from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 8 s. What is its acceleration?

formulas.name: SUVAT: displacement from initial velocity

variables.name: displacement
variables.description: Change in position along the line of motion.

formulas.explanation: On a velocity-time graph the displacement is the area under the line. With constant acceleration that area is a rectangle u t plus a triangle ½ × t × a t. The t² term is why falling objects cover more distance every second.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when the final velocity v is not known or not needed, for example for falling objects or a car starting from rest.
assumptions: no air resistance for free fall

example.story: A stone is dropped from rest down a well and hits the water after 3.0 s. How deep is the well (g = 9.81 m/s²)?

formulas.name: SUVAT: velocity and displacement (no time)

variables.name: final velocity
variables.description: Velocity after moving a displacement s.

formulas.explanation: Eliminating t between v = u + at and s = ut + ½at² gives this equation. It is the work-energy theorem in disguise: multiply by ½m and it says the change in kinetic energy equals force times distance.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when time is not given and not asked for, such as braking distances and the height reached by a ball thrown upwards.

example.story: A car travelling at 20 m/s brakes with a deceleration of 5 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?

formulas.name: SUVAT: displacement from average velocity
formulas.explanation: With constant acceleration the velocity changes evenly, so the average velocity is exactly halfway between u and v. Displacement is that average velocity times the time; on a v-t graph it is the area of a trapezium.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when the acceleration is not known or not needed.

example.story: A train speeds up evenly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 20 s. How far does it travel?

formulas.name: SUVAT: displacement from final velocity
formulas.explanation: This is the mirror image of s = ut + ½at²: it works backwards from the final velocity. Substituting u = v - at into that equation gives this form.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when the initial velocity is unknown and not needed, for example when an object comes to rest.

example.story: A car brakes steadily at 4 m/s² and stops after 5 s. How far did it travel while braking?

formulas.name: Range of a projectile

variables.name: range
variables.description: Horizontal distance travelled before landing at launch height.

variables.name: launch angle
variables.description: Angle above the horizontal, in radians.

variables.name: gravitational field strength
variables.description: Free-fall acceleration, 9.81 m/s² near Earth's surface.

formulas.explanation: The horizontal velocity v cos θ is constant while gravity brings the projectile back down after a flight time of 2v sin θ / g. Multiplying them and using 2 sin θ cos θ = sin 2θ gives the range. It is largest at 45 degrees, and complementary angles such as 30 and 60 degrees give the same range.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for how far a ball, jet of water or long jumper travels when landing at the starting height.
assumptions: lands at the same height it was launched from

example.story: A ball is kicked at 20 m/s at 45 degrees. How far away does it land?

formulas.name: Maximum height of a projectile

variables.name: maximum height
variables.description: Highest point above the launch height.

variables.name: launch angle
variables.description: Angle above the horizontal, in radians.

variables.name: gravitational field strength
variables.description: Free-fall acceleration, 9.81 m/s² near Earth's surface.

formulas.explanation: Only the vertical part of the velocity, v sin θ, carries the projectile upwards. At the top that vertical velocity is zero, so v² = u² + 2as gives 0 = v² sin²θ - 2gH.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for the peak height of a thrown or kicked object.

example.story: A ball is kicked at 20 m/s at 45 degrees. How high does it go?

formulas.name: Time of flight of a projectile

variables.name: time of flight
variables.description: Time until the projectile returns to launch height.

variables.name: launch angle
variables.description: Angle above the horizontal, in radians.

variables.name: gravitational field strength
variables.description: Free-fall acceleration, 9.81 m/s² near Earth's surface.

formulas.explanation: Vertically, the projectile starts at v sin θ upwards and gravity reduces this by g every second. It takes v sin θ / g to reach the top and the same time to come down again.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find how long a projectile is in the air, which then gives the range from the horizontal velocity.

example.story: A ball is kicked at 20 m/s at 45 degrees. How long is it in the air?

formulas.name: Newton's second law

variables.name: resultant force
variables.description: The net force on the object (all forces combined).

variables.name: acceleration
variables.description: Acceleration produced, in the direction of the force.

formulas.explanation: A resultant force makes a mass accelerate: double the force and the acceleration doubles, double the mass and it halves. One newton is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s². If the forces balance, the acceleration is zero and the object keeps moving at constant velocity (Newton's first law).
formulas.whenToUse: Use it whenever forces cause motion: cars, rockets, lifts, objects on slopes.

example.story: A resultant force of 3000 N acts on a 1200 kg car. What is its acceleration?

formulas.name: Weight

variables.name: weight
variables.description: The gravitational force on the object.

variables.name: mass
variables.description: Amount of matter, the same everywhere.

variables.name: gravitational field strength
variables.description: 9.81 N/kg on Earth, 1.62 N/kg on the Moon.

formulas.explanation: Weight is a force, measured in newtons, while mass is measured in kilograms. Weight is mass times the local gravitational field strength, so an astronaut has the same mass on the Moon but only about a sixth of the weight.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to turn a mass into the force of gravity on it, the first step in most force diagrams.
assumptions: uniform gravitational field near the surface

example.story: An astronaut of mass 65 kg stands on the Moon, where g = 1.62 N/kg. What is her weight?
steps: W = 105.3 N (on Earth it would be about 638 N)

formulas.name: Friction force

variables.name: friction force
variables.description: Force opposing sliding (or the maximum static friction).

variables.name: coefficient of friction
variables.description: Depends on the two surfaces; typically 0.1 to 1.

variables.name: normal force
variables.description: Force pressing the surfaces together, perpendicular to them.

formulas.explanation: Friction between dry surfaces is roughly proportional to how hard they are pressed together, and nearly independent of the contact area. The coefficient μ depends on the materials. Static friction can take any value up to μ_s F_N; once sliding, kinetic friction is μ_k F_N.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for blocks sliding on surfaces, braking, and the maximum force before something starts to slip.

example.story: A box pressed on the floor with a normal force of 50 N slides with μ = 0.4. What is the friction force?

formulas.name: Weight component down a slope

variables.name: force along the slope
variables.description: Component of weight pulling the object down the slope.

variables.name: slope angle
variables.description: Angle of the slope above the horizontal, in radians.

formulas.explanation: On a slope, the weight mg splits into a part along the slope, mg sin θ, and a part pressing into it, mg cos θ. The steeper the slope, the larger the part that pulls the object down it. The normal force equals mg cos θ when nothing else pushes into the slope.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for objects on ramps, hills and inclined planes, together with friction and Newton's second law.

example.story: A 10 kg crate sits on a ramp at 30 degrees. What force pulls it down the ramp?

formulas.name: Drag force

variables.name: drag force
variables.description: Air or fluid resistance opposing the motion.

variables.name: fluid density
variables.description: About 1.2 kg/m³ for air at room temperature.

variables.name: drag coefficient
variables.description: Depends on shape: about 0.3 for a car, 0.47 for a sphere, 1.0 to 1.3 for a person upright.

formulas.explanation: At everyday speeds, drag grows with the square of the speed: going twice as fast means four times the drag. The factor ½ρv² is the dynamic pressure of the oncoming fluid, and C_d A describes how much of it the shape catches. When drag equals weight, a falling object reaches terminal velocity.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for air resistance on cars, cyclists, skydivers and balls at moderate to high speeds.
assumptions: C_d roughly constant over the speed range

example.story: A car with C_d = 0.3 and frontal area 2.2 m² drives at 30 m/s through air of density 1.2 kg/m³. What is the drag force?

formulas.name: Hooke's law

variables.name: force
variables.description: Force stretching or compressing the spring.

variables.name: spring constant
variables.description: Stiffness: force needed per metre of extension.

variables.name: extension
variables.description: Change in length from the natural length.

formulas.explanation: Up to its limit of proportionality, a spring stretches in proportion to the force: double the force, double the extension. The spring constant k measures stiffness. The spring pulls back with an equal force, which is what makes springs oscillate.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for springs, elastic bands, newton meters and anything elastic within its proportional range.

example.story: A spring with k = 200 N/m holds a 15 N load. How far does it stretch?

formulas.name: Young's modulus

variables.name: Young's modulus
variables.description: Stiffness of the material itself, independent of shape.

formulas.explanation: Stress is force per area (F/A) and strain is fractional extension (ΔL/L). Their ratio, Young's modulus, is a property of the material: about 200 GPa for steel, 70 GPa for aluminium and 0.01 to 0.1 GPa for rubber. A thick, short wire stretches less, but its material has the same E.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to compare materials, or to predict how much a wire, rod or beam stretches under load.

example.story: A 2 m steel wire with cross-section 1 mm² stretches by 1 mm under a 100 N load. What is Young's modulus?

formulas.name: Pressure

variables.name: force
variables.description: Force acting at right angles to the surface.

variables.name: area
variables.description: Area the force is spread over.

formulas.explanation: Pressure is how concentrated a force is. The same force on a smaller area gives a bigger pressure, which is why knives are sharp and snowshoes are wide. One pascal is one newton per square metre.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for forces on surfaces: feet on the floor, pistons, tyres, and the pressure of fluids.
assumptions: force perpendicular to the surface and evenly spread

example.story: A person weighing 600 N stands on shoes with a total area of 0.04 m². What pressure do they exert on the floor?

formulas.name: Density

variables.name: mass
variables.description: Mass of the object or sample.

formulas.explanation: Density tells you how much mass is packed into each cubic metre. It is a property of the material, not of the object: a nail and a ship's hull of steel have the same density. Objects less dense than water float.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to identify materials, to convert between mass and volume, and to predict floating and sinking.

example.story: A metal block has a mass of 2.7 kg and a volume of 0.001 m³. What is its density, and what metal could it be?
steps: ρ = 2700 kg/m³, the density of aluminium

formulas.name: Pressure in a fluid

variables.name: pressure due to the fluid
variables.description: Extra pressure at depth h (add the air pressure on top for the total).

formulas.explanation: The fluid above any point has weight, and that weight per unit area is the pressure. A column of height h and area A has weight ρ A h g, so dividing by A gives ρ g h. Pressure depends only on depth, not on the shape of the container.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for divers, dams, water towers, blood pressure and barometers.

example.story: What is the water pressure on a diver 10 m below the surface of a lake?
steps: p = 98 100 Pa, almost one extra atmosphere

formulas.name: Archimedes' principle (buoyant force)

variables.name: fluid density
variables.description: Density of the fluid, not of the object.

formulas.explanation: An object in a fluid is pushed up with a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. The pressure on its bottom is greater than on its top, and the difference adds up to ρ V g. If this force is at least the object's weight, it floats.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for ships, balloons, hydrometers and finding the volume or density of irregular objects.

example.story: A 2 litre (0.002 m³) stone is fully under water. What upward force does the water exert on it?

formulas.name: Work done by a force

variables.name: angle
variables.description: Angle between force and displacement, in radians.

formulas.explanation: A force does work when it moves something. Only the part of the force along the motion counts, which is F cos θ. A force at right angles to the motion, such as the normal force on a level floor, does no work. One joule is one newton acting over one metre.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the energy transferred when pushing, pulling or lifting, especially at an angle.

example.story: A child pulls a sled 20 m with a force of 50 N along a rope at 30 degrees to the ground. How much work is done?

formulas.name: Kinetic energy
formulas.explanation: Kinetic energy is the work needed to bring a mass from rest up to speed v. Because it depends on v², doubling the speed quadruples the energy, which is why a car at 60 km/h needs four times the braking distance of one at 30 km/h.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it in energy conservation problems, collisions, braking and anything moving.

example.story: What is the kinetic energy of a 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m/s (72 km/h)?

formulas.name: Gravitational potential energy (near a surface)

variables.name: potential energy gained
variables.description: Energy stored by lifting the object.

formulas.explanation: Lifting a mass against its weight mg through a height h takes work mg × h, and that energy is stored as gravitational potential energy. It is released again as kinetic energy when the object falls. Only changes in height matter.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for lifting, falling, roller coasters, hydroelectric dams and pendulums near the Earth's surface.
assumptions: uniform g (heights small compared with the Earth's radius)

example.story: A 2 kg book is lifted onto a shelf 1.5 m higher. How much potential energy does it gain?

formulas.name: Elastic potential energy

variables.name: elastic energy
variables.description: Energy stored in the stretched or compressed spring.

variables.name: extension
variables.description: Stretch or compression from natural length.

formulas.explanation: The force needed to stretch a spring grows from 0 to kx, so the average force is ½kx. Work done is average force times distance, ½kx × x = ½kx². It is the area under the force-extension graph.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for catapults, trampolines, bows, springs in toys and oscillators.
assumptions: within the limit of proportionality (Hooke's law holds)

example.story: A spring with k = 200 N/m is compressed by 5 cm. How much energy does it store?

formulas.name: Power

variables.name: power
variables.description: Rate of doing work or transferring energy.

formulas.explanation: Power is how fast energy is transferred. One watt is one joule per second. Two lifts that raise the same load the same height do the same work, but the faster one has more power.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for engines, motors, people climbing stairs, and electrical appliances.
assumptions: average power over the time interval

example.story: A lift raises 600 kg through 20 m (117 720 J of work) in 30 s. What is its power output?

formulas.name: Power from force and velocity

variables.name: power
variables.description: Rate at which the force does work.

variables.name: force
variables.description: Force in the direction of motion.

formulas.explanation: Work is force times distance, and power is work per second, so power is force times distance per second, which is velocity. At top speed a car's engine power exactly balances the power lost to drag and friction.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for vehicles at steady speed, the power needed against drag, and conveyor belts.

example.story: A car moves at a steady 30 m/s against 500 N of resistive forces. What power must the engine deliver?

formulas.name: Efficiency

variables.name: efficiency
variables.description: Fraction of input energy or power that is useful (multiply by 100 for %).

formulas.explanation: No machine turns all its input energy into useful output; the rest is wasted, usually as heat. Efficiency is the useful fraction, always between 0 and 1. The same ratio works with energies or powers, as long as both are the same kind.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for motors, power stations, light bulbs and any energy conversion.
assumptions: input and output measured over the same time

example.story: A motor takes 750 W of electrical power and delivers 600 W of mechanical power. What is its efficiency?

formulas.name: Momentum

variables.name: momentum
variables.description: Mass in motion, a vector in the direction of v.

formulas.explanation: Momentum combines how much is moving with how fast. It is conserved in collisions and explosions when no outside force acts. Newton's second law can be written as force equals rate of change of momentum.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for collisions, recoil, rockets and anything where impacts matter.

example.story: A 0.16 kg cricket ball is bowled at 40 m/s. What is its momentum?

formulas.name: Impulse

variables.name: impulse
variables.description: Force times the time it acts; equals the change in momentum.

formulas.explanation: Impulse is the total push a force gives: force multiplied by how long it lasts. It equals the change of momentum it causes. Crumple zones, airbags and bending your knees on landing all increase Δt, so the same change of momentum needs a smaller force.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for impacts and collisions, and to read the area under a force-time graph.
assumptions: F is the average force over Δt

example.story: A foot pushes a ball with an average force of 1125 N for 0.01 s. What impulse does the ball receive?

formulas.name: Impulse-momentum theorem
formulas.explanation: Combining F = ma with a = (v - u)/Δt shows that force times time equals the change in momentum. It is the most general form of Newton's second law: force is the rate of change of momentum.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the average force in a short impact when you know the speeds before and after.
assumptions: F is the average resultant force

example.story: A 0.45 kg football at rest is kicked to 25 m/s. The foot is in contact for 0.01 s. What is the average force?

formulas.name: Conservation of momentum (two bodies)
formulas.explanation: When two bodies interact, Newton's third law says they push each other with equal and opposite forces for the same time. Their changes in momentum are therefore equal and opposite, so the total momentum stays the same. Velocities are signed: choose a positive direction.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for any collision, explosion or recoil where outside forces are negligible during the interaction.

example.story: A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits a 1 kg trolley at rest. Afterwards the 2 kg trolley moves at 1 m/s. How fast does the 1 kg trolley move?

formulas.name: Perfectly inelastic collision

variables.name: common final velocity
variables.description: Velocity of the joined bodies afterwards.

formulas.explanation: When two bodies stick together, they share one final velocity. Momentum is conserved, so the total momentum divided by the total mass gives that velocity. Kinetic energy is not conserved: some becomes heat, sound and deformation.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for crashes where vehicles lock together, a bullet embedding in a block, or coupling railway wagons.

example.story: A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s runs into a stationary 1500 kg car and they move off together. What is their speed just after the crash?

formulas.name: Centre of mass of two bodies
formulas.explanation: The centre of mass is the mass-weighted average position. It lies closer to the heavier body. Two bodies in orbit both circle their common centre of mass, called the barycentre.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for balance problems, stability, and the motion of systems such as binary stars or the Earth and Moon.
assumptions: point masses or bodies whose own centres are known

example.story: The Earth (5.9722 × 10²⁴ kg) and Moon (7.342 × 10²² kg) are 3.844 × 10⁸ m apart. How far from Earth's centre is their barycentre?
steps: x ≈ 4.67 × 10⁶ m, inside the Earth (radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m)

formulas.name: Centripetal acceleration

variables.name: centripetal acceleration
variables.description: Acceleration towards the centre of the circle.

formulas.explanation: Moving in a circle at constant speed is still acceleration, because the direction of the velocity keeps changing. The acceleration points to the centre and grows with the square of the speed. A tighter turn (smaller r) needs a bigger acceleration.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for cars on bends, satellites, centrifuges and anything going round.

example.story: A car drives round a bend of radius 50 m at 15 m/s. What is its centripetal acceleration?

formulas.name: Centripetal acceleration (angular form)
formulas.explanation: Substituting v = ωr into v²/r gives ω²r. For a spinning object, every point has the same ω, so the acceleration is largest at the rim. This is how a centrifuge separates samples.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when the rotation rate is known rather than the speed, as for spinning wheels, centrifuges and planets.

example.story: A point is 0.5 m from the centre of a platform spinning at 2 rad/s. What is its centripetal acceleration?

formulas.name: Centripetal force

variables.name: centripetal force
variables.description: Resultant force towards the centre needed for circular motion.

formulas.explanation: Newton's second law applied to centripetal acceleration gives the resultant inward force needed to keep an object on a circle. It is not a new kind of force: tension, friction, gravity or a normal force provides it. If it disappears, the object flies off along a tangent.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the tension in a whirled string, the friction needed on a bend, or the gravity holding a satellite in orbit.

example.story: A 0.5 kg ball on a 1.2 m string is whirled in a horizontal circle at 4 m/s. What tension is needed?

formulas.name: Angular velocity from period
formulas.explanation: One full turn is 2π radians, and it takes one period T. Dividing gives the angle turned per second. Angular velocity is the same for every point on a rigid rotating object.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to convert a rotation period into ω for circular motion and oscillation formulas.

example.story: The Earth turns once relative to the stars every 86 164 s. What is its angular velocity?

formulas.name: Angular frequency
formulas.explanation: Each cycle of a rotation or oscillation corresponds to 2π radians of phase. So f cycles per second is 2πf radians per second. Formulas for oscillations and AC circuits are usually neater in ω.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to convert frequency into angular frequency for simple harmonic motion, waves and AC circuits.

example.story: Mains electricity in Europe alternates at 50 Hz. What is its angular frequency?

formulas.name: Speed from angular velocity
formulas.explanation: In one second the object turns through ω radians, and an angle of ω radians on a circle of radius r is an arc of length ωr. So points further from the axis move faster even though they turn at the same rate.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to connect rotation rate with speed: wheels, gears, records, the Earth's surface.

example.story: A wheel of radius 0.3 m turns at 10 rad/s. How fast does a point on its rim move?

formulas.name: Period of a simple pendulum

variables.name: period
variables.description: Time for one complete swing (there and back).

variables.name: length
variables.description: Distance from the pivot to the centre of the bob.

formulas.explanation: For small swings, the restoring force on a pendulum is proportional to its displacement, so it moves in simple harmonic motion. The period depends only on the length and on g, not on the mass or (for small swings) on the amplitude. That is why pendulums were used in clocks.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for pendulum clocks, swings, measuring g in the lab, or a crane's swinging load.
assumptions: light string and a point-like bob

example.story: What is the period of a 1.0 m pendulum on Earth?

formulas.name: Period of a mass on a spring
formulas.explanation: Hooke's law gives a restoring force -kx, so a = -(k/m)x: simple harmonic motion with ω = √(k/m). A heavier mass oscillates more slowly and a stiffer spring faster. Unlike a pendulum, the period does not depend on g.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for springs, car suspensions, vibrating molecules and any system with a linear restoring force.

example.story: A 0.5 kg mass hangs on a spring with k = 20 N/m. What is its period of oscillation?

formulas.name: Simple harmonic motion: displacement

variables.name: time
variables.description: Time since release from x = A.

formulas.explanation: An object in simple harmonic motion moves back and forth like the shadow of a point going round a circle. Released from rest at x = A, its displacement follows a cosine curve. Velocity and acceleration are also sinusoidal, with the acceleration always pointing back towards equilibrium.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find where an oscillating mass, pendulum or vibrating object is at a given time.
assumptions: starts at maximum displacement (use sine if it starts at equilibrium)

example.story: A mass oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m at 1 Hz (ω = 2π rad/s), released from x = A at t = 0. Where is it at t = 0.125 s?

formulas.name: Simple harmonic motion: maximum speed
formulas.explanation: Differentiating x = A cos ωt gives v = -Aω sin ωt, whose largest size is Aω. The object moves fastest as it passes the middle and stops momentarily at the ends. The maximum acceleration is ω²A, at the ends.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for the top speed of oscillating systems, from tuning forks to earthquake-shaken buildings.

example.story: A mass on a spring oscillates with ω = 4 rad/s and amplitude 5 cm. What is its maximum speed?

formulas.name: Moment of a force

variables.name: moment
variables.description: Turning effect of the force about the pivot.

variables.name: perpendicular distance
variables.description: Shortest distance from the pivot to the line of the force.

formulas.explanation: The turning effect of a force depends on its size and how far from the pivot it acts, measured at right angles to the force. That is why a long spanner makes a stubborn nut easier to turn, and why door handles are far from the hinges.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for levers, spanners, seesaws, cranes and beams.
assumptions: d measured perpendicular to the line of action

example.story: A force of 40 N is applied at the end of a 0.25 m spanner, at right angles to it. What is the moment about the nut?

formulas.name: Principle of moments

variables.name: first force
variables.description: Force on one side of the pivot.

variables.name: first distance
variables.description: Perpendicular distance of F₁ from the pivot.

variables.name: second distance
variables.description: Perpendicular distance of F₂ from the pivot.

formulas.explanation: An object balances when the clockwise moments about any point equal the anticlockwise moments. With one force on each side of a pivot, that means force times distance is the same on both sides. A small force far from the pivot can balance a large force close to it.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for seesaws, balances, levers, wheelbarrows and beams in equilibrium.

example.story: On a seesaw, a child weighing 300 N sits 2 m from the pivot. Where must a child weighing 400 N sit to balance?

formulas.name: Torque

variables.name: lever arm length
variables.description: Distance from the axis to where the force acts.

variables.name: angle
variables.description: Angle between the lever arm and the force, in radians.

formulas.explanation: Only the part of the force perpendicular to the lever arm, F sin θ, turns the object. Pushing straight along the arm (θ = 0) does nothing; pushing at right angles gives the full rF. Torque is the cross product r × F.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for spanners, pedals, door handles and engines when the force is not at right angles.

example.story: A 50 N force pulls at 60 degrees to a 0.3 m wrench. What torque does it produce?

formulas.name: Rotational kinetic energy

variables.name: moment of inertia
variables.description: Resistance to changes in rotation; depends on mass and how far it is from the axis.

formulas.explanation: Every bit of a spinning object moves with speed ωr, so its kinetic energy is ½ m (ωr)². Adding over the whole object gives ½ I ω², where I = Σ m r². It is the rotational version of ½ m v².
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for flywheels, rolling objects, spinning tops and turbines.

example.story: A flywheel with moment of inertia 0.5 kg·m² spins at 10 rad/s. How much energy does it store?

formulas.name: Angular momentum
formulas.explanation: Angular momentum is the rotational version of linear momentum. With no outside torque it is conserved, so a skater who pulls in their arms (smaller I) spins faster (larger ω). The same law explains why collapsing stars spin up into fast pulsars.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for spinning skaters, divers, planets, gyroscopes and collisions involving rotation.
assumptions: rigid body rotating about a fixed axis

example.story: A wheel with moment of inertia 2 kg·m² spins at 3 rad/s. What is its angular momentum?

formulas.name: Newton's law of gravitation
formulas.explanation: Every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to both masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. Double the distance and the force drops to a quarter. G is tiny, so gravity is only noticeable when at least one mass is huge.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for forces between planets, moons, stars and satellites.
assumptions: point masses or spherically symmetric bodies
speeds and fields where general relativity is not needed

example.story: The Earth (5.9722 × 10²⁴ kg) and Moon (7.342 × 10²² kg) are 3.844 × 10⁸ m apart. How strongly do they attract each other?

formulas.name: Gravitational field strength of a planet

variables.name: field strength
variables.description: Gravitational force per kilogram (equal to the free-fall acceleration).

variables.name: distance from centre
variables.description: Distance from the planet's centre (its radius at the surface).

formulas.explanation: Dividing Newton's law of gravitation by the small mass m gives the force per kilogram, the field strength. At the Earth's surface it is about 9.8 N/kg. It falls with the square of the distance from the centre.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find g on other planets or at different heights above the Earth.

example.story: Calculate g at the Earth's surface from its mass 5.9722 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.371 × 10⁶ m.
steps: g ≈ 9.82 N/kg (rotation lowers the measured value slightly)

formulas.name: Orbital speed (circular orbit)

variables.name: orbital speed
variables.description: Speed needed for a circular orbit.

variables.name: central mass
variables.description: Mass of the body being orbited.

variables.name: orbit radius
variables.description: Distance from the centre of the central body.

formulas.explanation: In a circular orbit gravity provides exactly the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r. The satellite's own mass cancels, leaving v = √(GM/r). Higher orbits are slower.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for satellites, space stations, moons and planets in near-circular orbits.
assumptions: satellite mass much smaller than M

example.story: The International Space Station orbits about 408 km above the Earth, at r = 6.779 × 10⁶ m. How fast does it travel?

formulas.name: Escape velocity

variables.name: escape velocity
variables.description: Minimum launch speed to escape the gravity completely.

variables.name: mass of the body
variables.description: Mass of the planet or star.

variables.name: starting distance
variables.description: Distance from the centre at launch.

formulas.explanation: To escape, an object's kinetic energy must at least equal the energy needed to climb out of the gravitational well, GMm/r. Setting ½mv² = GMm/r gives the escape velocity, √2 times the orbital speed at the same radius.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for rockets, whether planets keep their atmospheres, and black holes (where it reaches c).

example.story: What is the escape velocity from the surface of the Earth?

formulas.name: Kepler's third law

variables.name: orbit radius
variables.description: Radius (or semi-major axis) of the orbit.

variables.name: central mass
variables.description: Mass of the body being orbited.

formulas.explanation: The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the orbit's size. Kepler found this from planetary data; Newton derived it by combining the orbital speed with v = 2πr/T. It also lets astronomers weigh stars and planets from their satellites' orbits.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the period or height of an orbit, such as a geostationary satellite, or the mass of a planet with a moon.
assumptions: circular orbit (or r = semi-major axis for an ellipse)
orbiting mass much smaller than M

example.story: A geostationary satellite orbits once per sidereal day, 86 164 s. What is the radius of its orbit?
steps: r ≈ 4.216 × 10⁷ m (about 35 800 km above the surface)

formulas.name: Gravitational potential energy (general)

variables.name: potential energy
variables.description: Energy relative to being infinitely far away (always negative).

variables.name: central mass
variables.description: Mass of the planet or star.

formulas.explanation: Far from a planet, gravity is not uniform, so mgh no longer works. Choosing zero energy at infinite distance, the potential energy at distance r is -GMm/r. It is negative because work must be done to pull the object away; mgh is the approximation of the change near the surface.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for satellites, escape velocity and any situation where the height change is comparable to the planet's radius.

example.story: What is the gravitational potential energy of a 1000 kg satellite orbiting 7.0 × 10⁶ m from the Earth's centre?
